scenes.tts: In an adult human, a litre of arterial blood carries about two hundred millilitres of oxygen. If that blood were plasma alone, it would carry about three. Oxygen dissolves poorly in water, and plasma is mostly water. So how does blood make up the difference?
scenes.visual: Two bars, blood about 200 mL and plasma alone about 3 mL, with a question mark for the gap.

scenes.tts: In mammals, almost all the oxygen rides on hemoglobin. That is an iron-containing protein packed inside red blood cells. Each human hemoglobin molecule has four chains and four oxygen-binding sites. Saturation is the fraction of those sites that hold oxygen.
scenes.visual: A red cell block holds a hemoglobin block of four chains with four sites; oxygen chips fill the sites; saturation reads 2 of 4 then 4 of 4.
scenes.narration: In mammals, almost all the oxygen rides on hemoglobin. That is an iron-containing protein packed inside red blood cells. Each human hemoglobin molecule has four chains and four oxygen-binding sites. Saturation is the fraction of those sites that hold oxygen.

scenes.tts: Plot saturation against P O two, and you get the oxygen dissociation curve. For adult human blood it is S-shaped. Above about sixty millimetres of mercury it is nearly flat, so blood in the lungs loads almost fully. Between about ten and forty it is steep, so a small fall in tissue P O two releases a lot of oxygen. The shape comes from cooperative binding. Oxygen at one site makes the other sites on that molecule bind more readily.

scenes.tts: Take an illustrative adult human at rest. Arterial P O two is about one hundred millimetres of mercury, at ninety-eight percent saturation. Mixed venous blood is near forty millimetres of mercury, at seventy-five percent. The tissues took twenty-four percent of the oxygen offered. With a cardiac output of five litres per minute, that is two hundred and forty millilitres of oxygen per minute. Three quarters of the oxygen comes back unused. That reserve sits on the steep part.
scenes.caption: Take an illustrative adult human at rest. Arterial PO2 is about 100 mmHg, at 98% saturation. Mixed venous blood is near 40 mmHg, at 75%. The tissues took 24% of the oxygen offered. With a cardiac output of 5 L per minute, that is 240 mL of oxygen per minute. Three quarters of the oxygen comes back unused. That reserve sits on the steep part.

scenes.tts: In Copenhagen in nineteen oh three, Christian Bohr and colleagues raised the carbon dioxide around fresh dog blood. At the same oxygen pressure, it held less oxygen. Today the Bohr effect names that fall in affinity when pH falls or carbon dioxide rises. The curve shifts right, and P fifty rises. Higher temperature and more B P G also shift it right.

scenes.tts: In respiring tissue, carbon dioxide is high and P O two is low. That is where the curve is steep. At the same P O two, a right-shifted curve holds less oxygen, so the blood has released more. In adult human blood, hemoglobin loads on the flat part and unloads on the steep part.
